title: Smallest Value in a Rotated List
statement:
A list of distinct integers was sorted ascending and then rotated: some number of items, possibly zero, were moved from the end to the front, keeping their order. For example, [2, 6, 9, 15, 19, 23] rotated by 3 becomes [15, 19, 23, 2, 6, 9].

You get the rotated list nums but not how far it was rotated. Return its smallest value.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.

examples.why: The list climbs to 23, drops to 2, then climbs again. The smallest value is right after the drop.
Rotated by zero, so there is no drop at all. A search that assumes a drop exists somewhere in the middle walks right and returns a wrong value.
Rotated by one: the drop sits between index 0 and 1, right at the edge of the search range.

constraints: nums is an ascending list rotated by 0 to n − 1 places
hints: Split the list at any index. At least one side is a normal sorted run. Which side holds the drop?
Compare nums[mid] with the last value nums[hi]. If nums[mid] is bigger, the values must drop somewhere after mid.
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the minimum is in (mid, hi], so lo = mid + 1. Otherwise the run from mid to hi is sorted and mid may be the minimum, so hi = mid. Stop when lo === hi.

explain.intuition:
The rotated list is two sorted runs: a high run followed by a low run, and the minimum is the first item of the low run. Every value in the high run is bigger than every value in the low run. So one comparison tells you which run mid is in: compare it with the last value of the range. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], mid is in the high run and the minimum lies to its right. If nums[mid] < nums[hi], mid is in the low run, so the minimum is mid or to its left.

Why the last value and not the first? Because the right end is always in the low run, even when the list is not rotated at all; then the "low run" is the whole list. The first value has no such guarantee: in [4, 8, 13, 21], nums[mid] > nums[lo] is true and still the minimum is on the left.
steps: Set lo = 0, hi = n − 1. Promise: the minimum is in [lo, hi].
While lo < hi (more than one candidate), take mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2). Rounding down keeps mid < hi, so nums[mid] and nums[hi] are different items.
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop is after mid: lo = mid + 1.
Otherwise mid is in the low run and may be the minimum: hi = mid.
pitfalls: Comparing with nums[lo] instead of nums[hi]. It cannot tell an unrotated list from one whose drop is to the right of mid.
Setting hi = mid − 1 in the else branch. mid itself may be the minimum, as in [21, 4, 8, 13] where the first mid is index 1.
Using while (lo <= hi) together with hi = mid. Once lo === hi, mid equals both and nothing moves, so the loop never ends.

solutions.title: Scan for the minimum
solutions.idea: Look at every value. O(n), ignores the structure.

solutions.title: Binary search against the right end
solutions.idea: nums[mid] > nums[hi] means mid is in the high run, so the minimum is to its right. Otherwise mid is in the low run and the minimum is at mid or to its left.

followups: Return how many places the list was rotated. How does that relate to the index you found?
Values may now repeat, as in [3, 3, 1, 3]. Which comparison stops telling you anything, and what is the worst-case time now?
